user:
Compare two research ideas for the SAME research problem and pick the stronger one.

Research problem: Can MVFA's few-shot fusion be made inductive — scoring each image on its own, without the test-set min-max normalisation of the released code — without losing AUROC, and does this give a threshold that transfers to unseen modalities? The inductive fusion standardises each branch with leave-one-out statistics of the K normal support images (each support's zero-shot map, and its few-shot map against a memory bank built from the other K-1 supports, pooled over patches and levels), adds the standardised branches, and pools the fused map with the mean of its top 2% pixels; the threshold is the 95th percentile of the supports' leave-one-out image scores. Primary outcome: image- and pixel-level AUROC of inductive versus transductive fusion on every held-out modality and K in {2, 4, 8, 16}. Motivating measurement: the spread of the transductive AUROC across random test subsets and at 10% and 50% prevalence. Secondary outcomes: sensitivity, realised specificity, F1 and expected calibration error at the support-derived threshold. We also record whether the few-shot baselines compared in the target paper (APRIL-GAN, WinCLIP) normalise over the test set in their public code, to judge how widely the finding applies.

A stronger idea is one whose proposed change acts on the SPECIFIC mechanism of the target method that causes the problem (here: the released MVFA code and its verified behaviour), rather than a generic improvement that would apply to any anomaly detector.

Judge on:
1. Specificity. Would this idea plausibly solve THIS problem in THIS method better than a generic alternative? A mechanism that applies equally to any model and any problem is WEAKER, not stronger, because it does not explain why it fixes this problem.
2. Evidence. Is the proposed mechanism supported by the cited literature or by verified properties of the code and the benchmark?
3. Testability. Does the idea make a concrete, falsifiable prediction that can be checked on BMAD with one Colab GPU?

Explicitly DO NOT reward: length or polish of the write-up, stacking many modules, vague "add an attention/adapter module" proposals, or ideas that need data, labels or compute that are not available.

Idea A:
TITLE: Neyman-Pearson likelihood-ratio scoring: a support-normal density against a cross-modality abnormal density learned on source data
SUMMARY: Score each test patch by the log-ratio between a density of 'generic abnormal' patch features learned from source modalities' abnormal images and a density of the target's support-normal patches, giving the most powerful per-image test at a chosen false-positive level.
HYPOTHESIS: Likelihood-ratio scores combining a target support-normal Gaussian and a source-abnormal Gaussian mixture improve image AUROC by at least 1.5 points over normal-only Fisher fusion on held-out BMAD modalities at K = 2 and K = 4, while the support-derived threshold keeps realised false positives within 5 points of nominal.
RATIONALE: Fisher-MVFA asks only 'how unusual is this patch for a normal image of this modality?', the classical one-class question. By the Neyman-Pearson lemma, the most powerful test at a fixed false-positive rate compares the likelihood under normal and under abnormal hypotheses. MVFA's adapted features are trained to make abnormal patches of all modalities move in a common 'abnormal' direction (alignment to the abnormal text anchor), so an abnormal density estimated on source modalities may transfer, while the normal density must come from the target supports. This turns the scoring problem into a two-sided test without target anomalies.
METHOD: 1) Abnormal model: on source modalities' abnormal images, collect adapted patch tokens from the top-2% patches (images with masks: true lesion patches, used only for source-side density fitting; images without masks: top-2% by zero-shot score), PCA to 64 dims (fitted on source), Gaussian mixture with 8 components. 2) Normal model: Ledoit-Wolf Gaussian on the target supports' patch tokens in the same PCA space. 3) Patch score = log p_abn(f) - log p_nor(f), summed over levels; image score = top-2% mean. 4) Threshold: 95th percentile of support LOO image scores. 5) Code: fit_abnormal_gmm.py, scoring.py lr_score(); no adapter retraining.
EXPERIMENT: BMAD leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); MVFA checkpoints selected on source-modality validation splits and the MVFA baseline re-run the same way; K in {2,4,8,16}; 3 seeds x 3 support draws, mean and std. Baselines: Fisher fusion; Mahalanobis normal-only; transductive MVFA. Ablations: number of components; abnormal model from images without masks only; PCA dimension. Metrics: image/pixel AUROC, realised FPR, sensitivity at the threshold. Falsification: AUROC gain below 0.5 points.

Idea B:
TITLE: Episode-trained fusion calibrator: learning how to fuse MVFA's branches from simulated few-shot episodes on source modalities
SUMMARY: Learn, on simulated K-shot episodes drawn from the source modalities' validation splits, a small calibrator that maps support statistics and per-image branch scores to an anomaly probability, then apply it unchanged to the unseen target modality.
HYPOTHESIS: A logistic calibrator trained on simulated few-shot episodes from the five source modalities, taking support-standardised branch scores and support-statistic features as input, reduces expected calibration error on the held-out modality by at least 30% relative to support-only LOO-Z fusion, with image AUROC within 1 point.
RATIONALE: Parent 1 (Fisher) calibrates against support normals but has no notion of what abnormal scores look like; parent 2 (Platt) learns a calibrator but from synthetic anomalies whose realism reviewers doubted. A different source of abnormal evidence is already available: the source modalities have real labelled normal and abnormal validation images. Simulating the deployment situation (K supports, unseen test images) on each source modality and learning how fused scores relate to labels transfers calibration knowledge across modalities without synthetic data or target labels — a meta-learning view of fusion.
METHOD: 1) For each source modality m and 200 episodes: sample K normal supports from valid/good of m; score 64 other validation images of m (balanced) with LOO-Z per-branch scores. 2) Features per image: [Z_zero top-2%, Z_few top-2%, Z_zero max, Z_few max, log K, support LOO score std per branch]. 3) Train logistic regression (L2, C = 1) on all episodes of all source modalities (target excluded). 4) Deployment on the target: compute features with its supports; p = sigmoid(w^T x + b). 5) Code: new script train_calibrator.py (uses MVFA checkpoints trained without the target), scoring.py apply_calibrator(). No adapter retraining.
EXPERIMENT: BMAD leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); MVFA checkpoints selected on source-modality validation splits and the MVFA baseline re-run the same way; K in {2,4,8,16}; 3 seeds x 3 support draws, mean and std. Baselines: LOO-Z with logistic mapping fitted on supports only; Fisher p-value fusion; synthetic-Platt calibration. Ablations: feature set; number of episodes; per-modality vs pooled calibrator. Metrics: ECE (15 bins), Brier score, AUROC, sensitivity at p = 0.5. Falsification: ECE reduction below 30% or AUROC loss above 2 points.

Respond in exactly this format:
REASONING: <one to three sentences explaining your choice>
CONFIDENCE: <HIGH | MEDIUM | LOW>
WINNER=<A | B | TIE>
